claim: CD28 is essential for activation of helper T cells.
source: The co-stimulatory molecule CD28 is essential for activation of helper T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge

claim: Continued CD28 expression is important for effector CD4+ T cells following infection.
source: We show that continued CD28 expression is important for effector CD4+ T cells following infection
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Maintained CD28 is required for the expansion of T helper type 1 cells during viral infection.
source: maintained CD28 is required for the expansion of T helper type 1 cells, and for the differentiation and maintenance of T follicular helper cells during viral infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 6

claim: Maintained CD28 is required for the differentiation and maintenance of T follicular helper cells during viral infection.
source: maintained CD28 is required for the expansion of T helper type 1 cells, and for the differentiation and maintenance of T follicular helper cells during viral infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5

claim: Persistent CD28 is required for clearance of Citrobacter rodentium from the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Persistent CD28 is also required for clearance of the bacterium Citrobacter rodentium from the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 9

claim: CD28 persistence is required for helper T cell polarization in response to infection.
source: Together, this study demonstrates that CD28 persistence is required for helper T cell polarization in response to infection, describing a novel function for CD28 that is distinct from its role in T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings

claim: T cell activation requires peptide-MHC:TCR interaction and a co-stimulatory signal.
source: T cell activation requires two signals: peptide in the context of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) interacting with the T cell receptor (TCR), and a co-stimulatory signal (Lafferty and Cunningham, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: CD28 binding to CD80/CD86 initiates a transcriptional program that enables effective T cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: The binding of CD28 to its ligands, CD80/CD86, initiates a transcriptional program that enables effective T cell proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28 function

claim: In the absence of CD28 signaling, T cells fail to respond and become anergic.
source: In the absence of CD28 signaling T cells fail to respond, and become anergic (Diehn et al., 2002; Riley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 signaling is essential for CD4+ T cell proliferation.
source: CD28 signaling is essential for multiple facets of CD4+ T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992), including proliferation, survival (Boise et al., 1995), glucose metabolism (Frauwirth et al., 2002), and migration (Marelli-Berg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 signaling is essential for CD4+ T cell survival.
source: CD28 signaling is essential for multiple facets of CD4+ T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992), including proliferation, survival (Boise et al., 1995), glucose metabolism (Frauwirth et al., 2002), and migration (Marelli-Berg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 signaling is essential for CD4+ T cell glucose metabolism.
source: CD28 signaling is essential for multiple facets of CD4+ T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992), including proliferation, survival (Boise et al., 1995), glucose metabolism (Frauwirth et al., 2002), and migration (Marelli-Berg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 signaling is essential for CD4+ T cell migration.
source: CD28 signaling is essential for multiple facets of CD4+ T cell activation (Harding et al., 1992), including proliferation, survival (Boise et al., 1995), glucose metabolism (Frauwirth et al., 2002), and migration (Marelli-Berg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28-deficient mice have reduced expansion of effector CD4+ T cells after infection or immunization.
source: Consequently, CD28-deficient mice have reduced expansion of effector CD4+ T cells and do not form T helper type 1 (Th1) and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells after infection or immunization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28-deficient mice

claim: CD28-deficient mice do not form Th1 cells after infection or immunization.
source: Consequently, CD28-deficient mice have reduced expansion of effector CD4+ T cells and do not form T helper type 1 (Th1) and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells after infection or immunization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28-deficient mice

claim: CD28-deficient mice do not form Tfh cells after infection or immunization.
source: Consequently, CD28-deficient mice have reduced expansion of effector CD4+ T cells and do not form T helper type 1 (Th1) and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells after infection or immunization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28-deficient mice

claim: Tfh cells provide growth and differentiation signals to germinal center B cells.
source: Tfh cells provide growth and differentiation signals to germinal center B cells, enabling them to exit the germinal center as long-lived plasma cells or memory B cells (Crotty, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: Th1 cells are formed during a Type 1 immune response and facilitate the clearance of intracellular pathogens.
source: Th1 cells are formed during a Type 1 immune response and facilitate the clearance of intracellular pathogens (Zhu and Paul, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: Impaired formation of Tfh and Th1 cells results in impaired cellular and humoral immunity to foreign antigens in CD28-deficient mice.
source: Impaired formation of Tfh and Th1 cells results in impaired cellular and humoral immunity to foreign antigens in CD28-deficient mice (Shahinian et al., 1993; Green et al., 1994; Ferguson et al., 1996; King et al., 1996; Mittrucker et al., 1996; Walunas et al., 1996; Walker et al., 1999; Bertram et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations

claim: The expression of CD28 and its ligands increases progressively after priming.
source: The expression of CD28 and its ligands increases progressively after priming, raising the possibility that CD28 signaling is utilized during the effector phase of the immune response.
evidence: This is an observation that leads to a hypothesis

claim: CD28-deficient helper T cells do not become activated.
source: CD28-deficient helper T cells do not become activated, and thus cannot be used to evaluate the role for CD28 after T cell priming.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28-deficient T cells

claim: CD28 has two ligands, CD80 and CD86, which it shares with CTLA-4.
source: Moreover, CD28 has two ligands, CD80 and CD86, which it shares with the inhibitory receptor cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD28 ligands

claim: CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells with age in primates but not rodents.
source: The role for CD28 on activated T cells is particularly pertinent as CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells with age, in HIV infection, and in the number of immune disorders in primates (but not rodents) (Weng et al., 2009; Aberg, 2012; Broux et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells in HIV infection in primates but not rodents.
source: The role for CD28 on activated T cells is particularly pertinent as CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells with age, in HIV infection, and in the number of immune disorders in primates (but not rodents) (Weng et al., 2009; Aberg, 2012; Broux et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells in immune disorders in primates but not rodents.
source: The role for CD28 on activated T cells is particularly pertinent as CD28 expression is lost on a proportion of activated T cells with age, in HIV infection, and in the number of immune disorders in primates (but not rodents) (Weng et al., 2009; Aberg, 2012; Broux et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can impair the germinal center response.
source: Studies have suggested that CD28 may play a role following T cell priming, for example blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can impair the germinal center response (Han et al., 1995)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: Blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can prolong graft survival.
source: Studies have suggested that CD28 may play a role following T cell priming, for example blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can impair the germinal center response (Han et al., 1995), prolong graft survival, and suppress autoimmunity (Salomon and Bluestone, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: Blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can suppress autoimmunity.
source: Studies have suggested that CD28 may play a role following T cell priming, for example blocking CD28 ligands during an ongoing immune response can impair the germinal center response (Han et al., 1995), prolong graft survival, and suppress autoimmunity (Salomon and Bluestone, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation

claim: OX40 is a co-stimulatory molecule that is induced after T cell priming.
source: To generate a strain of mice where CD28 is lost after T cell priming, we took advantage of the expression pattern of OX40 (encoded by the Tnfrsf4 gene), a co-stimulatory molecule that is induced after T cell priming (Mallett et al., 1990; Gramaglia et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: 48 hours following immunization, both OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ control and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells had undergone up to four cell divisions.
source: 48 hr following immunization both OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ control and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells had undergone up to four cell divisions, as measured by dilution of cell trace violet
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Around 30% of activated OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ cells had lost CD28 expression 48 hours following immunization.
source: 48 hr following immunization both OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ control and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells had undergone up to four cell divisions, as measured by dilution of cell trace violet, and around 30% of activated OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+cells had lost CD28 expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Both OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ control and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells produced IL-2 48 hours following immunization.
source: Both OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ control and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells produced IL-2, consistent with activation via CD28 (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1D

claim: IL-2 was produced by Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells irrespective of whether they have maintained or lost CD28 expression.
source: Importantly, IL-2 was produced by Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells irrespective of whether they have maintained (CD28+) or lost CD28 expression (CD28−), suggesting that CD28− cells have indeed been activated through CD28 signaling prior to induction of OX40cre (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: There was equivalent induction of ICOS on OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells 48 hours following immunization.
source: There was also equivalent induction of the Inducible T-cell COStimulator (ICOS), a molecule whose expression is dependent on CD28 signaling (McAdam et al., 2000), and the T cell activation marker CD44 on OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: There was equivalent induction of CD44 on OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells 48 hours following immunization.
source: There was also equivalent induction of the Inducible T-cell COStimulator (ICOS), a molecule whose expression is dependent on CD28 signaling (McAdam et al., 2000), and the T cell activation marker CD44 on OT-II Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+ and OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: ICOS and CD44 were expressed at similar levels on CD28+ and CD28− cells from the OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cell population.
source: Furthermore, both ICOS and CD44 were expressed at similar levels on CD28+ and CD28− cells from the OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cell population (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F

claim: Around half of the activated CD4+ T cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had lost CD28 expression.
source: OX40cre expression is largely restricted to the CD4+ T cell compartment (Klinger et al., 2009) and around half of the activated (CD44high) cells expressed Cre and had lost CD28 expression (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: 15–20% of naïve CD4+ T cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice have expressed OX40cre and had lost CD28.
source: Furthermore, 15–20% of naïve (CD44low) cells have expressed OX40cre and had lost CD28 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had comparable basal serum immunoglobulin to heterozygous control animals.
source: CD28-deficient mice have impaired basal serum titers of IgG1 and IgG2a and germinal center formation after immunization (Shahinian et al., 1993; Ferguson et al., 1996), by contrast Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had comparable basal serum immunoglobulin (Figure 1I) to heterozygous control animals
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice formed germinal centers 7 days after sheep red blood cell immunization.
source: CD28-deficient mice have impaired basal serum titers of IgG1 and IgG2a and germinal center formation after immunization (Shahinian et al., 1993; Ferguson et al., 1996), by contrast Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had comparable basal serum immunoglobulin (Figure 1I) to heterozygous control animals, and formed germinal centers 7 days after sheep red blood cell immunization (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J

claim: 5 days post influenza infection, approximately 50% of activated CD4+ T cells had lost CD28 expression in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice.
source: In the early phase of the infection, 5 days post infection, ∼50% of activated CD4+ T cells had lost CD28 expression (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: IL-2 production was intact in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 5 days post influenza infection.
source: In the early phase of the infection, 5 days post infection, ∼50% of activated CD4+ T cells had lost CD28 expression (Figure 2A), IL-2 production was intact (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: There were comparable proportions of proliferating cells in the medLN of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice compared to controls 5 days post influenza infection.
source: In the early phase of the infection, 5 days post infection, ∼50% of activated CD4+ T cells had lost CD28 expression (Figure 2A), IL-2 production was intact (Figure 2B), and there were comparable proportions of proliferating cells in the medLN (Figure 2C) of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice compared to controls
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: There were comparable numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh-precursors in the draining lymph node of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice and heterozygous controls 5 days post influenza infection.
source: At this time point, there were comparable numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh-precursors (Figure 2D) and IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 2E) in the draining lymph node of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice and heterozygous controls, demonstrating that T cell priming was intact.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: There were comparable numbers of IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells in the draining lymph node of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice and heterozygous controls 5 days post influenza infection.
source: At this time point, there were comparable numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh-precursors (Figure 2D) and IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 2E) in the draining lymph node of Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice and heterozygous controls, demonstrating that T cell priming was intact.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh cells 12 days post influenza infection.
source: However, 12 days post infection, Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh cells (Figure 2D) and IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 2E) in the medLN and Th1 cells in the lungs (Figure 2F) compared to control mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells in the medLN 12 days post influenza infection.
source: However, 12 days post infection, Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh cells (Figure 2D) and IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 2E) in the medLN and Th1 cells in the lungs (Figure 2F) compared to control mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of Th1 cells in the lungs 12 days post influenza infection.
source: However, 12 days post infection, Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice had reduced numbers of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh cells (Figure 2D) and IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ Th1 cells (Figure 2E) in the medLN and Th1 cells in the lungs (Figure 2F) compared to control mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: There were fewer Bcl-6+Ki-67+B220+ germinal center B cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 12 days post influenza infection.
source: Corresponding to a deficit in Tfh cells, there were fewer Bcl-6+Ki-67+B220+ germinal center B cells (Figure 2G) in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: 30–40% of Tfh cells had lost CD28 expression in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 12 days following influenza infection.
source: Expression of CD28 on Tfh in the medLN and Th1 cells in the lung was determined 12 days following influenza infection: 30–40% of Tfh cells (Figure 2H) and 55–65% of lung Th1 cells (Figure 2I) had lost CD28 expression in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: 55–65% of lung Th1 cells had lost CD28 expression in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 12 days following influenza infection.
source: Expression of CD28 on Tfh in the medLN and Th1 cells in the lung was determined 12 days following influenza infection: 30–40% of Tfh cells (Figure 2H) and 55–65% of lung Th1 cells (Figure 2I) had lost CD28 expression in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I

claim: T cells derived from Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ stem cells are outcompeted during the response to influenza A virus.
source: In contrast, in the CD45.1 Cd28+/flox Ox40cre/+: CD45.2 Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ chimeras the CD45.2+ cells barely contributed to the Tfh or Th1 cell populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This demonstrated that T cells derived from Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ stem cells are outcompeted during the response to influenza A virus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Approximately 50% of the transferred OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells had lost CD28 expression 3.5 days after immunization.
source: 3.5 days after immunization ∼50% of the transferred OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells had lost CD28 expression (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells formed fewer CXCR5+Bcl-6+ Tfh-precursors than heterozygous control OT-II T cells 3.5 days after immunization.
source: OT-II Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ T cells formed fewer CXCR5+Bcl-6+ Tfh-precursors than heterozygous control OT-II T cells (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3E

claim: 90% of the CD4+ T cells that had a CXCR5+Bcl-6+ pre-Tfh phenotype were CD28+ 3.5 days after immunization.
source: Furthermore, 90% of the CD4+ T cells that had a CXCR5+Bcl-6+ pre-Tfh phenotype were CD28+ (Figure 3D,E), demonstrating that T cells that have lost CD28 are less able to differentiate into Tfh cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E

claim: Both apoptosis and cell division were similar between CD28+ and CD28− cells 3.5 days after immunization.
source: Both apoptosis and cell division were similar between CD28+ and CD28− cells (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G

claim: ICOS expression was reduced on pre-Tfh cells that had lost CD28.
source: However, ICOS expression was reduced on pre-Tfh cells that had lost CD28 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Blocking CD80/86 after T cell priming impaired the formation of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh-precursors.
source: This impaired the formation of CXCR5+Bcl-6+CD4+ Tfh-precursors (Figure 3I), supporting data from Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice showing that CD28 signaling is required after T cell priming for Tfh differentiation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I

claim: The percentage of Tfh cells that had lost CD28 expression decreased over time during the response to influenza.
source: We observed that the percentage of Tfh cells that had lost CD28 expression decreased over time during the response to influenza (Figure 4A,B), suggesting that Tfh maintenance is impaired by the loss of CD28.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: There was an increase in the number of apoptotic Tfh cells 14 days after influenza infection in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice compared with heterozygous controls.
source: Consistent with this, there was an increase in the number of apoptotic Tfh cells 14 days after influenza infection in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice compared with heterozygous controls (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The increase in apoptotic Tfh cells was most pronounced in the cells that had lost CD28 expression.
source: Consistent with this, there was an increase in the number of apoptotic Tfh cells 14 days after influenza infection in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice compared with heterozygous controls (Figure 4C), and this was most pronounced in the cells that had lost CD28 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: There was an increase in proliferation of Tfh cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 14 days after influenza infection.
source: There was also an increase in proliferation of Tfh cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: There was a decrease in expression of Bcl-XL in Tfh cells that had lost CD28.
source: There was also a decrease in expression of two molecules downstream of CD28; the pro-survival molecule Bcl-XL (Figure 4E) and the costimulatory molecule ICOS (Figure 4F) in Tfh cells that had lost CD28.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: There was a decrease in expression of ICOS in Tfh cells that had lost CD28.
source: There was also a decrease in expression of two molecules downstream of CD28; the pro-survival molecule Bcl-XL (Figure 4E) and the costimulatory molecule ICOS (Figure 4F) in Tfh cells that had lost CD28.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Expression of CD44 was equivalent between CD28+ and CD28− Tfh cells.
source: Expression of the activation marker CD44, on the other hand, was equivalent between these cell types (Figure 4G) suggesting that activation is intact.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Halving the amount of Bcl-XL was not sufficient to cause increased Tfh cell death and reduced Tfh number during influenza A virus infection.
source: However, halving the amount of Bcl-XL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E) or ICOS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H) alone was not sufficient to cause increased Tfh cell death and reduced Tfh number during influenza A virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E

claim: Halving the amount of ICOS was not sufficient to cause increased Tfh cell death and reduced Tfh number during influenza A virus infection.
source: However, halving the amount of Bcl-XL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E) or ICOS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H) alone was not sufficient to cause increased Tfh cell death and reduced Tfh number during influenza A virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H

claim: The percentage of Bcl-6+Ki67+B220+ germinal center B cells was not altered between mice that received isotype control or CD80/86 blocking antibodies 15 days post influenza infection.
source: 15 days post infection the percentage of Bcl-6+Ki67+B220+ germinal center B cells was not altered between mice that received isotype control or CD80/86 blocking antibodies (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The proportion of Tfh cells was reduced after anti-CD80/86 treatment 15 days post influenza infection.
source: 15 days post infection the percentage of Bcl-6+Ki67+B220+ germinal center B cells was not altered between mice that received isotype control or CD80/86 blocking antibodies (Figure 5B), but the proportion of Tfh cells was reduced after anti-CD80/86 treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: There was an increase in Tfh cell apoptosis after anti-CD80/86 treatment 15 days post influenza infection.
source: There was an increase in Tfh cell apoptosis and decreased Bcl-XL and ICOS expression (Figure 5D–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: There was decreased Bcl-XL expression in Tfh cells after anti-CD80/86 treatment 15 days post influenza infection.
source: There was an increase in Tfh cell apoptosis and decreased Bcl-XL and ICOS expression (Figure 5D–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: There was decreased ICOS expression in Tfh cells after anti-CD80/86 treatment 15 days post influenza infection.
source: There was an increase in Tfh cell apoptosis and decreased Bcl-XL and ICOS expression (Figure 5D–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: There was a decrease in Tfh cell proliferation after anti-CD80/86 treatment 15 days post influenza infection.
source: however, in contrast with these results there was a decrease in Tfh cell proliferation (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G

claim: The proportion of CD28-negative Th1 cells in the lung remained constant between 5 and 14 days post influenza infection.
source: The proportion of CD28-negative Th1 cells in the lung remained constant between 5 and 14 days post influenza infection (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that, unlike Tfh, continued CD28 expression is dispensable for Th1 maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B

claim: Blocking CD80/86 at d11 and 13 post infection did not affect the proportion of Th1 cells in the medLN or lung 15 days post infection.
source: Consistent with this, blocking CD80/86 at d11 and 13 post infection did not affect the proportion of Th1 cells in the medLN or lung (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) 15 days post infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: A smaller proportion of IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ medLN Th1 cells was detected in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice at 7 days post infection.
source: A smaller proportion of IFNγ+CD44highCD4+ medLN Th1 cells was detected in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice (Figure 6C) at 7 days post infection
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ CD44highCD4+ cells showed normal apoptosis 7 days following infection.
source: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ CD44highCD4+ cells showed normal apoptosis (Figure 6E), but a decrease in proliferation (Figure 6F) 7 days following infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ CD44highCD4+ cells showed a decrease in proliferation 7 days following infection.
source: Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ CD44highCD4+ cells showed normal apoptosis (Figure 6E), but a decrease in proliferation (Figure 6F) 7 days following infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: The proportion of IL-2 secreting cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice was decreased 7 days following infection.
source: Consistent with this, the proportion of IL-2 secreting cells in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice was decreased (Figure 6G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Upregulation of CXCR3 was impaired in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 7 days following infection.
source: Upregulation of CXCR3, a tissue homing receptor expressed on Th1 cells (Beima et al., 2006) was also impaired (Figure 6H) in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: The proportion of CXCR3+CD62LlowCD4+ cells was reduced in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 7 days following infection.
source: Upregulation of CXCR3, a tissue homing receptor expressed on Th1 cells (Beima et al., 2006) was also impaired (Figure 6H) in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice, and the proportion of CXCR3+CD62LlowCD4+ cells was reduced (Figure 6I)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: There were fewer Th1 cells in the lung in Cd28flox/flox Ox40cre/+ mice 7 days following infection.
